analysis.one_liner: Slashes capital gains tax to 6% for one year and indexes investment gains for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Ways and Means Committee with 2 cosponsors until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut the tax rate on capital gains to 6% for both individuals and corporations for one year after enactment, with a 3% rate for low- and middle-income taxpayers, and applied a reduced rate to the alternative minimum tax [S2][S3]. Separately, it would have permanently adjusted the tax basis of corporate stock and business property for inflation, so investors would not pay tax on gains that merely reflect rising prices [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which controls tax legislation, and never advanced [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People and companies selling appreciated assets. The temporary 6% rate would apply to gains realized during a one-year window, encouraging holders of stock, businesses, and real estate to sell and pay far less tax than the then-current rates; the permanent indexing provision would keep letting holders of stock and tangible business property subtract inflation from their taxable gains going forward [S2][S3]. Because capital gains are concentrated among higher-income households, the largest dollar benefits would go to those households, though the bill's 3% rate nominally extends to low- and middle-income taxpayers with gains [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Holders of stocks and appreciated assets

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the individual capital gains tax rate to 6%, and to 3% for the portion of gains falling in lower income brackets, on gains realized during a one-year moratorium period after enactment [S2][S3].
Applies the same 6% temporary rate to corporate capital gains and reduces the alternative minimum tax on gains during the same window [S2][S3].

Permanently indexes the tax basis of corporate stock and tangible business property to the gross national product deflator, so gains caused purely by inflation are not taxed when assets held more than one year are sold [S2][S3].

Extends the indexing benefit through pass-through vehicles — mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, S corporations, partnerships — so investors in those vehicles receive the adjustment at the entity level [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through reduced Treasury revenue. Taxpayers without capital gains — most wage earners — would get little direct benefit from a capital gains rate cut, and the lost revenue would have to be made up through other taxes, borrowing, or reduced spending. The permanent indexing provision would compound that revenue loss every year, with the largest reductions accruing to the households and corporations holding the most appreciated assets [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers through lost federal revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill would sharply reduce federal revenue at a time when the government was running deficits, with the benefit concentrated among households and corporations that own appreciated assets; taxpayers without such assets would receive little direct benefit [S2].

A one-year temporary rate cut rewards those wealthy enough to choose when to sell, since holders could delay or accelerate sales to land inside the moratorium window, while taxpayers with little flexibility gain less [S3].

Indexing only the basis of assets without indexing depreciation, interest deductions, or other tax items gives investors a one-sided adjustment, and the bill excludes some assets — creditor interests, options, net lease property, most foreign stock — creating lines that similar assets fall on either side of [S3].

An honest supporter would concede that the deepest cuts (6% and 3%) apply to gains recognized in a single year, so the biggest benefits would flow to the largest portfolios rather than to typical workers, whose main asset — a home's ordinary appreciation — is not covered by the indexing provision as drafted [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is that lower capital gains taxes and inflation indexing reduce a real tax distortion: under current law, inflation is taxed as if it were gain. But this bill's design would deliver most of its benefit to the households and corporations with the largest appreciated portfolios, through a one-year fire-sale rate and a permanent indexing provision, while the revenue cost would be borne broadly. The temporary 6% rate in particular functions as a targeted window for large asset holders to cash out cheaply. On balance the provisions tilt heavily toward concentrated wealth relative to the public benefit they purchase.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, the committee that writes tax law, and it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Jon Kyl introduced the Window of Opportunity Act on September 21, 1993, with the bill referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
The bill attracted 2 cosponsors, both Republicans [S4].
Kyl delivered introductory remarks on the measure on October 20, 1993 [S5].
No further action is recorded: the bill never left committee and received no vote in either chamber before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, no tax change occurred: the Treasury kept the revenue that the rate cut and indexing would have foregone, and holders of appreciated assets did not receive the reduced rates. Ordinary taxpayers were spared the shifted tax burden; investors gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Jon Kyl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 21, 1993 and delivered introductory remarks a month later.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; the bill's sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans, and it never advanced to a vote where bipartisan positions could be measured [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would cut the tax on stock gains to 6% for one year and permanently index stock basis for inflation, with pass-through treatment for mutual funds and other investment vehicles. Its gain comes from revenue the Treasury would not collect, a cost spread across all taxpayers, while the benefit concentrates in households that own stock.

Corporate capital gains would be taxed at 6% during the moratorium period, and the alternative minimum tax on gains would be reduced. Like the individual benefit, this is a revenue loss funded by other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Real estate and business asset holders
industries.note: Tangible business property held more than one year would get inflation-indexed basis, lowering taxable gain on sales of buildings, equipment, and land (with exclusions for net lease property and related-party deals). The benefit accrues to asset owners; the revenue cost is public.
